captions.instagram:
How does a bathroom shower work?

A shower makes no warm water of its own: it mixes two streams and throws the result through sixty tiny holes. See the mixing sum, the wax capsule and the sliding spool that stop it scalding you, and why a rain shower dribbles under an overhead tank.

→ How does a shower work? Cold water falls from a tank on the roof. A branch of it goes through the geyser.
→ Hot and cold meet in the wall mixer. A diverter sends the mix to the spout, the head or the hand shower.
→ A shower does not make warm water. It mixes hot water from the geyser with cold water from the tank.
→ Open another cold tap and less cold reaches the mixer, so the shower jumps hotter.
→ A pressure-balancing spool slides towards the weaker side and pinches the stronger one, so the mix holds.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/showerclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a bathroom shower work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A shower makes no warm water of its own: it mixes two streams and throws the result through sixty tiny holes. See the mixing sum, the wax capsule and the sliding spool that stop it scalding you, and why a rain shower dribbles under an overhead tank.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/showerclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/showerclear

In this video:
• Two pipes in, three ways out. Cold water comes down from the overhead tank, and a branch of it goes through the geyser.
• Warm water is a sum. Outlet temperature = (hot flow × hot temperature + cold flow × cold temperature) ÷ total flow.
• A spool that balances pressure. A pressure-balancing valve has a piston that slides towards whichever side is weaker and pinches the stronger one.
• Wax that feels the water. A thermostatic valve keeps a capsule of wax in the mixed water.
• Holes turn pressure into speed. Nozzles trade pressure for speed: 0.14 bar inside a needle head throws jets out at 4.5 metres a second, and surface tension beads them into drops about 16 cm below.
• Litres, units and scalds. Water used is litres a minute times minutes: eight minutes at 9 L/min is 72 litres, five buckets, against one for a bucket bath.
